17.7.name: 17.07.md
17.7.text:
In this example, we needed to return multiple values from findBook. Here, a tuple makes most sense--a pair would suffice too, though it is less suitable for the task. With a tuple we can create a temporary "structure" to hold data of different types, which we could then store into our vector of vectors. Thereafter, the "structure" is not needed and would be disposed of.

That said, if we intended to use the tuple more often in our code, it is best to have used a dedicated struct. The advantage of struct over a tuple (or a pair) is that it makes the code easier to read, extend and maintain.

17.8.name: 17.08.md
17.8.text: The starting point (i.e. value) for the accumulate algorithm would be an empty object of type Sales_data. Given that the + operator of Sales_data ignores the string data member of the object, accumulate would return an object with the proper calculation performed for the particular book but leaves the bookNo variable untouched, i.e. leaves it as an empty string.

17.9.name: 17.09.md
17.9.text:
```cpp
(a) bitset<64> bitvec(32);
(b) bitset<32> bv(1010101);
(c) string bstr; cin >> bstr; bitset<8>bv(bstr);
```

(a) bitvec is initialized with 32ULL--the integral value 32 is implicitly

```text
converted to unsigned long long (p. 732). bit 0 to 5 will have the pattern
1 0000 (32 in base 10) and the rest of the bits till bit 63 will be 0.
```

(b) 1010101 (base 10) is F69B5 (base 16), which is at least 20 bits.

```text
Initializing bv with F69b5 will set the lower-order bits to 1111 0110 1001
1011 0101 and bits 21 to 31 to 0.
```

(c) bv will be initialized from the string bstr, which is initiated from the

```text
standard input. If bstr size is less than 8, the remaining higher order
bits will be set to 0. If its size is bigger than 8, the extra bits will be
discarded.
```
